stories.title: Commissioner's statement on facial recognition consultation response
stories.summary: Statement on the government's consultation response on the use of facial recognition and similar technologies in law enforcement. The Biometrics and Surveillance Camera Commissioner, Professor William Webster, said: I welcome the government’s response to its consultation on facial recognition and similar biometric technologies. It marks an important step towards primary legislation that will provide a clear legal basis for their use, protect the public and build confidence in how these technologies are deployed. Biometric surveillance technologies, including live facial recognition, are intrusive and conflict directly with fundamental human rights, including rights associated with freedom of movement, freedom of expression, the right to peaceful assembly and the right to privacy. The government’s response acknowledges the potential to interfere with these rights, and from my perspective clear legislation and effective safeguards are essential to mitigate these risks.
stories.why_it_matters: Following UK news can help us ask informed questions about life around us.

stories.title: The Last Ice on Puncak Jaya
stories.summary: Ice near the summit of the Indonesian mountain peak has shrunk to scattered patches too small to flow like glaciers. On the island of New Guinea, Indonesia’s Sudirman Range is one of the few places near the equator that have long held ice year-round. But near the summit of Puncak Jaya, the ice has dwindled to patches too small to flow like glaciers. Positioned in the tropics beside the largest expanse of warm ocean water on Earth, the range’s glaciers lie near the warmest conditions in which ice can survive year-round. Scientists have described these glaciers as high-altitude “ canaries in the coal mine ,” alongside other tropical ice such as the remnants of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, and the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania.

stories.title: Five further Critical Third Parties designated
stories.summary: HM Treasury has designated five further third-party suppliers as Critical Third Parties. HM Treasury has designated five further third-party suppliers as Critical Third Parties (CTPs): This brings the total number of designated CTPs to nine and represents the second cohort of a rolling programme. HM Treasury previously designated four major global cloud services and technology providers as Critical Third Parties (CTPs) in July 2026. The designations mean the Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority will work together to jointly oversee the critical services the CTPs provide to the financial sector, helping reduce the risk of widespread disruption and strengthening collaboration across the financial services ecosystem. Regulatory oversight applies only to specific systemic services provided to the financial sector, for example certain technology platforms and services, not firms’ entire operations. The government expects the overall number of designations to remain small, reflecting the regime’s proportionate approach to identifying only the most systemic third-party services.

on_this_day.title: The Suez Canal opens
on_this_day.summary: The Suez Canal officially opened on 17 November 1869. Located in Egypt, it connects the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea. Ships using the canal can travel between these seas without sailing around southern Africa. The opening was a significant moment in the history of maritime transport. The canal also has a complex political history, showing how a piece of infrastructure can matter to both travel and international affairs.
